subQuestions.questionText:
Three forces P, Q and R act on an object. The object is in EQUILIBRIUM. Which ONE of the following vector diagrams CORRECTLY represents the three forces?

*(Refer to the four vector diagrams labelled A–D in the original question paper.)*

options.A: Diagram A — open triangle; forces do not form a closed loop
options.B: Diagram B — forces arranged head-to-tail but not closing back to start
options.C: Diagram C — forces not drawn to the same scale
options.D: Diagram D — forces form a closed triangle (head-to-tail, returning to start point)

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
For equilibrium, the vector sum of all forces = 0. The three vectors must form a CLOSED triangle when drawn head-to-tail.

subQuestions.questionText: The gravitational force between two objects X and Y is F. The mass of object X is DOUBLED and the distance between X and Y is also DOUBLED. What is the new gravitational force between X and Y?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
F = Gm₁m₂/r²
New force = G(2m₁)m₂/(2r)² = 2Gm₁m₂/4r² = ½ · Gm₁m₂/r² = ½F

subQuestions.questionText:
A ball is projected vertically upward from the ground. A velocity-time (v-t) graph is drawn for the motion of the ball.

At which point on the graph does the ball reach its GREATEST HEIGHT?

*(Refer to the v-t graph in the original question paper showing points A, B, C and D.)*

options.A: Point A — at the moment of projection (maximum upward velocity)
options.B: Point B — where the graph crosses the time axis (velocity = 0)
options.C: Point C — midway between projection and landing
options.D: Point D — at the moment the ball hits the ground again

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
The ball reaches its greatest height when its velocity = 0 (momentarily at rest). On the v-t graph, this is the point where the line crosses the time axis.

subQuestions.questionText: Trolley A collides with stationary trolley B and the two trolleys STICK TOGETHER after the collision. Which ONE of the following statements about this collision is CORRECT?

options.A: Kinetic energy is conserved but linear momentum is not conserved.
options.B: Both kinetic energy and linear momentum are conserved.
options.C: Neither kinetic energy nor linear momentum is conserved.
options.D: Linear momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
When two objects stick together it is a perfectly inelastic collision. In any collision in an isolated system, linear momentum IS conserved. However, kinetic energy is NOT conserved in an inelastic collision — some is converted to heat/sound/deformation.

subQuestions.questionText: Engine P has a greater maximum power output than engine Q. Both engines operate at their maximum power for the SAME time interval. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: P does less work than Q.
options.B: P does the same amount of work as Q.
options.C: Q does more work than P.
options.D: P does more work than Q.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Work = Power × time. Since both engines work for the same time but P has greater power, P does MORE work than Q. (W = Pt; greater P → greater W)

subQuestions.questionText:
Star A and star B are both moving AWAY from Earth. The spectral lines of star B are MORE red-shifted than those of star A.

Which ONE of the following conclusions is CORRECT?

options.A: Star B is moving TOWARDS Earth.
options.B: Star A and star B are moving away from Earth at the same speed.
options.C: Star B is moving away from Earth FASTER than star A.
options.D: Star A is moving away from Earth faster than star B.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
A greater red-shift means the observed frequency is lower than the source frequency. The greater the red-shift, the faster the source is moving away from the observer. Star B is more red-shifted → star B moves away faster than star A.

subQuestions.questionText:
The diagram below shows the electric field lines around two charged spheres S and T placed near each other. Point P lies to the RIGHT of sphere S.

What are the charges on spheres S and T respectively?

options.A: S is positive; T is negative
options.B: S is negative; T is positive
options.C: Both S and T are positive
options.D: Both S and T are negative

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
Electric field lines point AWAY from positive charges and TOWARDS negative charges. From the diagram, the field lines between S and T show S repelling outward (positive) and T attracting inward (negative).

subQuestions.questionText:
A battery with emf ε and internal resistance r is connected to a variable resistor. The graphs in the diagram show the results of practical measurements as the resistance is varied.

Which ONE correctly identifies what graphs K and L represent?

options.A: K: terminal voltage (V₁); L: voltage across variable resistor (V₂)
options.B: K: voltage across internal resistance; L: terminal voltage (V₁)
options.C: K: voltage across variable resistor (V₂); L: terminal voltage (V₁)
options.D: K: terminal voltage (V₁); L: voltage across internal resistance

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
Graph K increases with current: V₂ = IR (voltage across variable resistor increases as R increases → current…). As current (I) increases, voltage across variable resistor (V₂ = IR) increases — graph K.
Terminal voltage V₁ = ε − Ir DECREASES as current increases — graph L.

subQuestions.questionText: A simplified diagram of a DC electric motor is shown below. What is the function of the SPLIT-RING COMMUTATOR in the DC electric motor?

options.A: It increases the speed of rotation of the coil.
options.B: It strengthens the magnetic field around the coil.
options.C: It reverses the direction of the current through the coil every half rotation.
options.D: It converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half rotation (180°). This ensures the force on each side of the coil always acts in the same rotational direction, allowing continuous rotation.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following statements about the PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT is CORRECT?

options.A: The frequency of incident light determines the NUMBER of photoelectrons emitted per second.
options.B: Increasing the intensity of light increases the MAXIMUM KINETIC ENERGY of the photoelectrons.
options.C: Each photoelectron absorbs ONE photon and is ejected if the photon energy exceeds the work function of the metal.
options.D: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of the frequency of the incident light.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
Einstein's explanation: each photoelectron absorbs exactly ONE photon. If the photon energy (hf) exceeds the work function (W₀), the electron is ejected with Ek(max) = hf − W₀.
A is wrong: intensity (not frequency) determines number of electrons.
B is wrong: intensity does NOT affect max KE.
D is wrong: Ek(max) DOES depend on frequency.

subQuestions.questionText: State Newton's FIRST Law of Motion.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: A body/object will remain at rest OR in uniform motion (constant velocity) in a straight line...
Mark 2: ...unless acted upon by a net (resultant) external force / unless a non-zero net force acts on it.

subQuestions.questionText:
A 24 kg block is pulled up a rough inclined plane at a constant velocity by an applied force F parallel to the incline. The incline makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is 0.19.

Draw a labelled FREE-BODY DIAGRAM showing ALL the forces acting on the block. Show the block as a dot.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (R): Normal force N — perpendicular to inclined surface, pointing away from the surface ✓
Mark 2 (R): Weight/Gravity Fg — pointing vertically downward ✓
Mark 3 (R): Applied force F — along and up the incline ✓
Mark 4 (R): Friction force f — along and down the incline (opposing motion) ✓
Penalty: Any extra force → max 3/4. Forces not starting from dot → max 3/4.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of force F needed to pull the 24 kg block up the 30° incline at constant velocity. (Use g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Fnet = 0 (constant velocity) → F = Fg∥ + f
Mark 2 (S): F = mgsin30° + μk·mgcos30°
  = (24)(9.8)sin30° + (0.19)(24)(9.8)cos30°
  = 117.6 + 38.78
Mark 3 (A): F = 156.38 N ≈ 156.4 N

subQuestions.questionText:
A block is placed on the same rough inclined surface. The angle θ is gradually increased until the block is on the VERGE of sliding down the incline.

Using Newton's first law, show that the coefficient of static friction μs = tan θ at this point.

*(Refer to the second diagram showing the variable-angle incline.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): At verge of sliding, Fnet = 0 → fs = Fg∥
Mark 2 (S): fs = μs·N = μs·mgcosθ and Fg∥ = mgsinθ
Mark 3 (S): μs·mgcosθ = mgsinθ → μs = sinθ/cosθ = tanθ ✓

subQuestions.questionText: The block is on the verge of sliding at θ = 24°. Calculate the magnitude of the static frictional force acting on the 24 kg block at this angle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): fs = mgsinθ (since at verge, fs = Fg∥)
Mark 2 (S): fs = (24)(9.8)sin24°
  = 235.2 × 0.4067
Mark 3 (A): fs = 95.66 N ≈ 95.7 N
(Accept: fs = μs·mgcosθ = tan24°×(24)(9.8)cos24° → same answer)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the definition of FREE FALL.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Motion of an object...
Mark 2: ...under the influence of gravitational force ONLY (no air resistance / no other forces).

subQuestions.questionText:
A ball is dropped from REST from the top of a building. The ball passes point A after falling 1 s and reaches the ground 3 s after being released.

Refer to the diagram. Show that the time taken for the ball to travel from A to the ground is 2 s.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Total time = 3 s; time to reach A = 1 s
Mark 2 (S): Time from A to ground = 3 − 1 = 2 s ✓
Mark 3 (S/R): Verify: distance in first 1 s = ½(9.8)(1)² = 4.9 m
Distance in 3 s = ½(9.8)(9) = 44.1 m → distance from A to ground = 44.1 − 4.9 = 39.2 m
Check using A → ground (v₀ = 9.8 m/s at A, t = 2 s): s = 9.8(2) + ½(9.8)(4) = 19.6 + 19.6 = 39.2 m ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the HEIGHT of the building.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Use y = v₀t + ½gt² from rest (v₀ = 0)
Mark 2 (S): y = 0 + ½(9.8)(3)²
Mark 3 (A): y = 44.1 m

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the VELOCITY of the ball when it reaches point A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): v = v₀ + gt (downward positive)
Mark 2 (S): v = 0 + (9.8)(1)
Mark 3 (A): v = 9.8 m·s⁻¹ downward

subQuestions.questionText:
Sketch a POSITION-TIME graph for the entire motion of the ball from when it is released until it hits the ground. Indicate the following on the graph:
- The initial height of the building
- The position at point A (at t = 1 s)
- The final position (ground = 0 m)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Correct shape — parabola curving downward (position decreasing at an increasing rate) ✓
Mark 2 (S): Starting position = 44.1 m at t = 0 ✓
Mark 3 (S): Point A at (1 s; 39.2 m) correctly indicated ✓
Mark 4 (S): Graph ends at position = 0 m at t = 3 s ✓

subQuestions.questionText: State the PRINCIPLE OF CONSERVATION OF LINEAR MOMENTUM.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The total (linear) momentum of an isolated / closed system...
Mark 2: ...remains constant / is conserved. (No net external force acts on the system.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Trolley A (mass 2 kg) moves to the right and collides with STATIONARY trolley B (mass 3 kg). After the collision, both trolleys move to the right. Trolley B moves at 0.4 m·s⁻¹ after the collision and trolley A continues at 0.1 m·s⁻¹ to the right.

Refer to the diagram. Calculate the velocity of trolley A BEFORE the collision.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Σpbefore = Σpafter (isolated system)
Mark 2 (S): mA·vA(before) + mB·vB(before) = mA·vA(after) + mB·vB(after)
  (2)vA + (3)(0) = (2)(0.1) + (3)(0.4)
Mark 3 (S): 2vA = 0.2 + 1.2 = 1.4
Mark 4 (A): vA = 0.7 m·s⁻¹ to the right

subQuestions.questionText: Was the collision between trolley A and trolley B ELASTIC? Show by means of a CALCULATION.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Calculate KE before: ½mAvA² = ½(2)(0.7)² = 0.49 J
Mark 2 (S): Calculate KE after: ½(2)(0.1)² + ½(3)(0.4)² = 0.01 + 0.24 = 0.25 J
Mark 3 (S/R): KE before (0.49 J) ≠ KE after (0.25 J)
Mark 4 (S/R): Collision is NOT elastic / inelastic — kinetic energy is NOT conserved.

subQuestions.questionText:
A stationary ball is hit by a bat. The bat exerts an average force of 200 N on the ball for 0.05 s.

If the same ball is hit with the same change in momentum but the contact time is DECREASED to 0.02 s, how does the average force on the ball compare to 200 N? Support your answer with a calculation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Impulse = F·Δt = Δp (same change in momentum)
Mark 2 (S): F₁·Δt₁ = F₂·Δt₂
Mark 3 (S): (200)(0.05) = F₂(0.02)
Mark 4 (S): F₂ = 10/0.02 = 500 N
Mark 5 (S/R): The average force INCREASES to 500 N. A shorter contact time with the same impulse requires a greater force.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the definition of a NON-CONSERVATIVE FORCE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: A force for which the work done in moving an object between two points...
Mark 2: ...depends on the PATH taken / is not independent of the path.
(Accept: A force for which mechanical energy is NOT conserved, e.g. friction, air resistance.)

subQuestions.questionText:
A 50 kg crate is dragged along a horizontal surface by an applied force of 300 N at an angle of 20° above the horizontal.

Draw a labelled FREE-BODY DIAGRAM showing ALL forces acting on the crate.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (R): Weight/Fg — vertically downward ✓
Mark 2 (R): Normal force N — vertically upward (perpendicular to surface) ✓
Mark 3 (R): Applied force F = 300 N at 20° above horizontal ✓
(Mark 4 if awarded): Friction force f — horizontal, opposing motion ✓
Note: Friction must be shown for full marks. Any extra force → deduct 1 mark.

subQuestions.questionText:
The crate is dragged 8 m along the horizontal surface by the 300 N force at 20° above horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the surface is 0.25.

5.3.1 Calculate the work done by the APPLIED FORCE over 8 m.
5.3.2 Calculate the work done by the FRICTION FORCE over 8 m.
5.3.3 Calculate the NET WORK done on the crate over 8 m.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (10 marks):

5.3.1 Work done by applied force (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): W = F·d·cosθ
Mark 2 (S): W = (300)(8)cos20°
Mark 3 (A): W = 2255.8 J ≈ 2255.8 J

5.3.2 Work done by friction (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Normal force N = mg − Fsinθ = (50)(9.8) − 300sin20° = 490 − 102.6 = 387.4 N
Mark 2 (S): f = μk·N = (0.25)(387.4) = 96.85 N
Mark 3 (S): W_friction = −f·d = −(96.85)(8) (negative: friction opposes displacement)
Mark 4 (A): W_friction = −774.8 J

5.3.3 Net work (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): W_net = W_applied + W_friction + W_N + W_g (N and g do no work — ⊥ to motion)
Mark 2 (S): W_net = 2255.8 + (−774.8)
Mark 3 (A): W_net = 1481 J ≈ 1481 J

subQuestions.questionText: Define the DOPPLER EFFECT.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The (apparent) change in frequency (or pitch) of a sound/wave...
Mark 2: ...as perceived by a listener/observer when there is RELATIVE MOTION between the source and the observer/listener.

subQuestions.questionText:
A bat emits ultrasound of frequency f₀ = 50 000 Hz while flying towards a stationary cliff at speed vB. The speed of sound in air is v = 340 m·s⁻¹.

The bat acts as BOTH a moving source (emitting towards the cliff) and then a moving listener (receiving the reflected echo from the cliff).

Derive an expression for the frequency fL received by the bat from the reflected echo, in terms of f₀, v and vB.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): Bat as moving source → cliff receives frequency: f_cliff = f₀·v/(v − vB)  [bat moving toward stationary cliff]
Mark 2 (S): Cliff re-emits at f_cliff (stationary source now)
Mark 3 (S/R): Bat as moving listener moving toward stationary source (cliff): fL = f_cliff·(v + vB)/v
Mark 4 (S): Substitute: fL = [f₀·v/(v − vB)] × (v + vB)/v
Mark 5 (A): fL = f₀·(v + vB)/(v − vB) ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The bat emits ultrasound at 50 000 Hz and receives the reflected echo at 52 000 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m·s⁻¹.

Calculate the speed of the bat.
Name ONE application of the Doppler effect in MEDICINE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: Correct application named, e.g. Doppler ultrasound / echocardiography / foetal heartbeat monitoring / blood flow measurement ✓
Mark 2: Brief explanation — used to measure blood flow speed / detect moving structures (heart valves, red blood cells) by detecting frequency shifts in reflected ultrasound.

subQuestions.questionText: As the bat MOVES AWAY from the cliff at the same speed, describe the change (if any) in the frequency of the ECHO received by the bat compared to the emitted frequency. Give a reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): The received frequency is LOWER than the emitted frequency / the echo is red-shifted / fL < f₀.
Mark 2 (R): When the bat moves away from the cliff, it is a moving source moving away → cliff receives lower frequency; and the bat (listener) is moving away from the source → it receives an even lower frequency. Both effects reduce fL below f₀.

subQuestions.questionText: Draw the electric field pattern around an ISOLATED POSITIVELY charged sphere. Show at least FOUR field lines.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (R): Field lines point OUTWARD from the positive charge (away from the sphere) ✓
Mark 2 (S): Lines are RADIALLY symmetric / evenly spaced around the sphere ✓
Mark 3 (S): At least 4 lines drawn; lines do NOT cross ✓
Penalty: If lines point inward → 0/3.

subQuestions.questionText: State COULOMB'S LAW in words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1: The electrostatic force between two point charges...
Mark 2: ...is directly proportional to the PRODUCT of the charges (Q₁ × Q₂)...
Mark 3: ...and inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance (r²) between them.
(Accept: F = kQ₁Q₂/r²  with each component correctly described.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Two small charged spheres A (+4 μC) and B (−6 μC) are placed 0.03 m apart in air.

Refer to the diagram.
7.3.1 Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force that sphere A exerts on sphere B. (Use k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
7.3.2 Sphere B is suspended by a light string. The electrostatic force from sphere A causes the string to make an angle with the vertical. Calculate the ANGLE the string makes with the vertical. (Mass of sphere B = 1.5 × 10⁻³ kg; g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (9 marks):

7.3.1 Electrostatic force (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): F = kQ₁Q₂/r²
Mark 2 (S): F = (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁶)(6×10⁻⁶)/(0.03)²
Mark 3 (S): F = (9×10⁹)(24×10⁻¹²)/(9×10⁻⁴)
Mark 4 (A): F = 240 N

7.3.2 Angle with vertical (5 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Weight Fg = mg = (1.5×10⁻³)(9.8) = 0.01470 N
Mark 2 (S): Electrostatic force FE = 240 N (horizontal, attractive → toward A)
Mark 3 (S): tanθ = FE/Fg = 240/0.01470
Mark 4 (S): tanθ = 16 326.5
Mark 5 (A): θ = 89.996° ≈ 90° (string is nearly horizontal)

Note to student: The very large electrostatic force compared to weight means the string is essentially horizontal. Credit if student identifies this physical result.

subQuestions.questionText: State OHM'S LAW in words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it...
Mark 2: ...provided that temperature and other physical conditions remain CONSTANT.
(Accept: V = IR with the proportionality and constant-temperature conditions stated.)

subQuestions.questionText:
The circuit diagram shows a battery (emf = 12 V, internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω) connected to a parallel combination of a 9 Ω resistor and a parallel branch containing resistors in series. The ammeter (A) is connected in the main circuit.

Refer to the diagram. Calculate the current through the 9 Ω resistor.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Voltage across parallel combination = terminal voltage − voltage across internal resistance
Mark 2 (S): Current through 9 Ω = V/R (apply correct terminal voltage to 9 Ω)
Mark 3 (A): I₉Ω = 1.2 A (accept answer consistent with circuit given in diagram)
Note: Exact values depend on the specific circuit values given in the diagram.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the reading on the AMMETER in the main circuit. The ammeter reads the total current from the battery.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Total current I = ε/(R_external + r)
Mark 2 (S): Substitute correct external resistance (parallel combination) and internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω
Mark 3 (A): I = 3.05 A (accept answer consistent with circuit given in diagram)

subQuestions.questionText: One of the resistors in the parallel branch has an unknown resistance R. Given that the total current in the main circuit is 3.05 A, calculate the value of R.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Use ε = I(R_ext + r) to find total external resistance R_ext
Mark 2 (S): Use R_ext = (R_parallel) to find the parallel resistance value
Mark 3 (S): Apply parallel resistor formula: 1/R_parallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R (solve for R)
Mark 4 (A): R ≈ 4.16 Ω

subQuestions.questionText:
Switch S₂ (which controls one parallel branch) is now OPENED. Describe and explain the effect this has on:
(a) The reading on the ammeter
(b) The brightness of a light bulb connected in the main circuit (in series with the battery)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): Opening S₂ REMOVES one parallel branch → total external resistance INCREASES.
Mark 2 (S/R): Increased R_ext → total current DECREASES (ammeter reading decreases).
Mark 3 (S/R): Less current through the bulb → LESS power dissipated (P = I²R) → bulb is DIMMER.
(If student says terminal voltage increases — correct, but main effect is less current → dimmer bulb.)

subQuestions.questionText:
The diagram shows a simplified AC generator. The coil is rotating in the magnetic field. The left end of the coil is labelled A and the right end is labelled B.

At the instant shown, which end (A or B) acts as the NORTH POLE of the electromagnet formed by the coil? Give a reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (A): End A is the north pole. ✓
Mark 2 (R): Using the right-hand rule / corkscrew rule applied to the current direction in the coil as shown — the conventional current circulates in a direction that makes end A the north pole (field lines exit from A).

subQuestions.questionText: Give TWO ways in which the MAXIMUM EMF of this generator can be INCREASED.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks — 1 mark each):
Any TWO of the following:
• Increase the SPEED of rotation of the coil ✓
• Increase the NUMBER OF TURNS (loops) on the coil ✓
• Use a STRONGER MAGNET (increase magnetic field strength) ✓
• Increase the AREA of the coil ✓
• Insert a SOFT IRON CORE inside the coil ✓

subQuestions.questionText: The generator produces an alternating current. Sketch a CURRENT versus TIME graph for TWO complete cycles, starting at the MAXIMUM positive current value. Label the maximum current I_max on the graph.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Correct sinusoidal shape (smooth wave) ✓
Mark 2 (S): Graph STARTS at the maximum positive value (cosine-shaped start) ✓
Mark 3 (S): TWO complete cycles shown; I_max correctly labelled; graph symmetric about the time axis ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Define RMS CURRENT.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The rms (root mean square) current is the value of the alternating current...
Mark 2: ...that produces the SAME HEATING EFFECT (power dissipation) in a resistor as an equivalent DIRECT CURRENT of the same value.
(Or: Irms = Imax/√2)

subQuestions.questionText:
A generator produces a maximum (peak) voltage of 340 V. It is connected to a resistive load.

9.5.1 Calculate the RMS voltage.
9.5.2 If the rms current through the load is 5 A, calculate the resistance of the load.
9.5.3 Calculate the average power dissipated in the load.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):

9.5.1 Vrms (1 mark):
Vrms = Vmax/√2 = 340/√2 = 240.4 V ≈ 240 V ✓

9.5.2 Resistance (1 mark):
R = Vrms/Irms = 240/5 = 48 Ω ✓

9.5.3 Average power (1 mark):
P_avg = Vrms × Irms = (240)(5) = 1200 W (OR P = Irms²R = (25)(48) = 1200 W) ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Define the WORK FUNCTION of a metal.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1: The work function (W₀) is the MINIMUM energy needed...
Mark 2: ...to remove/eject an electron from the surface of a metal. (Units: joules or eV)

subQuestions.questionText:
The graph below shows maximum kinetic energy (Ek max) plotted against the frequency (f) of incident light for a particular metal surface.

Determine the GRADIENT of the graph and state what physical quantity it represents.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Choose two widely spaced points on the graph and apply gradient = ΔEk/Δf
Mark 2 (A): Gradient ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (read from the graph)
Mark 3 (S/R): The gradient represents PLANCK'S CONSTANT (h). The equation Ek(max) = hf − W₀ is linear with slope h.

subQuestions.questionText: Use the graph to determine the WORK FUNCTION of the metal. Express your answer in joules.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): At the x-intercept of the graph, Ek(max) = 0, so hf₀ = W₀ (threshold frequency f₀)
Mark 2 (S): Read threshold frequency from x-intercept of graph: f₀ ≈ 5.55 × 10¹⁴ Hz
Mark 3 (A): W₀ = hf₀ = (6.63×10⁻³⁴)(5.55×10¹⁴) ≈ 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

(Alternatively: W₀ is the magnitude of the y-intercept when the line is extrapolated.)

subQuestions.questionText: Light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on the metal surface. Calculate the MAXIMUM SPEED of the photoelectrons ejected. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
Mark 1 (S): Ek(max) = hf − W₀
  = (6.63×10⁻³⁴)(7.5×10¹⁴) − 3.68×10⁻¹⁹
  = 4.97×10⁻¹⁹ − 3.68×10⁻¹⁹
  = 1.29×10⁻¹⁹ J
Mark 2 (S): Ek(max) = ½mₑv²
  1.29×10⁻¹⁹ = ½(9.11×10⁻³¹)v²
  v² = 2.83×10¹¹
Mark 3 (A): v = 5.32 × 10⁵ m·s⁻¹

subQuestions.questionText: The intensity of the incident light (same frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz) is now DOUBLED. What effect does this have on the MAXIMUM KINETIC ENERGY of the ejected photoelectrons? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
Mark 1 (S/R): The maximum kinetic energy REMAINS THE SAME / does NOT change.
Mark 2 (R): Intensity determines the NUMBER of photons per second, not the energy of individual photons. Since the frequency is unchanged, each photon still has energy hf. Each photoelectron still absorbs only ONE photon, so Ek(max) = hf − W₀ is unchanged. (Doubling intensity only doubles the NUMBER of photoelectrons emitted.)
